abstract.section_purpose: state policy question, data, method, findings and implication
abstract.key_claim: Between May 2021 and May 2025, U.S. renewable electricity generation industries paid about 11.5 percent less per hour than fossil fuel and nuclear generation for workers in the same detailed occupation; the gap was concentrated in solar, wind, geothermal and biomass (not hydroelectric) generation and in plant-operations and maintenance occupations, and it did not narrow while renewable generation employment doubled.

introduction.section_purpose: frame puzzle between green-premium and legacy-premium evidence and preview contribution
introduction.key_claim: No study compares the same occupation across generation sources within one industry over 2021-2025
blueprint_obligations: puzzle: green-premium claims vs legacy pay
gap in literature naming closest prior work (Curtis and Marinescu 2023; Colmer et al. 2025; Godoy and Isaksen 2025)

literature review and theory.section_purpose: evaluate prior studies, build rent-sharing framework with rivals, state H1-H5 as written in the theory stage
literature review and theory.key_claim: Establishment wage-setting predicts lower renewable pay for the same occupation; skills scarcity predicts higher
required_evidence: published green and brown premia from prior studies
forbidden_moves: mentioning this paper's own empirical output
blueprint_obligations: evaluate prior studies' strengths and weaknesses

data and methods.section_purpose: document data, sample descent, measures by role, estimating equations and inference
data and methods.key_claim: Occupation-by-year fixed effects compare the same job across industries
blueprint_obligations: data source and OEWS design (six panels over three years, MB3)
sample construction with counts (2,096 cells -> 1,876 analytic)
variables: outcome, focal predictor, moderators, fixed effects, weights

results.section_purpose: interpret Tables 1-5 and Figures 1-4 in hypothesis order
results.key_claim: Between May 2021 and May 2025, U.S. renewable electricity generation industries paid about 11.5 percent less per hour than fossil fuel and nuclear generation for workers in the same detailed occupation; the gap was concentrated in solar, wind, geothermal and biomass (not hydroelectric) generation and in plant-operations and maintenance occupations, and it did not narrow while renewable generation employment doubled.
forbidden_moves: ranking occupation groups by individual p-values

discussion.section_purpose: adjudicate theories, reconcile literature, state limitations
discussion.key_claim: Evidence most consistent with establishment wage-setting
blueprint_obligations: adjudicate rent-sharing vs skills-scarcity vs compensating differentials

conclusion.key_claim: Wages follow employer institutions more than technology
required_evidence: published literature cited in this section
blueprint_obligations: policy implications for just-transition and labor standards
